column2: The Flags Return to the Streets

News of the peace has passed from the ministries into the streets. Flags hang from balconies, musicians lead processions, and children imitate the soldiers returning from the campaign. Municipal councils arrange receptions for the troops, while families wait for men whose regiments have not yet come home. The rejoicing is real, but the ministers must now turn a victory proclamation into ordinary government in the newly acquired provinces. Public enthusiasm will not settle their accounts or reconcile every local grievance. For the moment, the crown and the country share the celebration of a war brought to a victorious close.
Receive the returning regiments and honour their service.

Italian administration at Tripoli has brought requests from scholars, surveyors and museum directors. Along the coast, ancient remains lie beside settlements whose inhabitants have their own rights and livelihoods. The ministry is asked to arrange journeys, record monuments and protect discoveries from private removal. Provincial officials warn that an archaeological mission must respect cultivated land, places of worship and local ownership. The court instructs its civil officers to hear these petitions through the ordinary administration. The remains of an older Mediterranean world may become a subject of study, but possession of the province does not make every monument the private property of the conqueror.
Entrust the petitions to the provincial civil authorities.
